palette_summary: warm sand and papyrus cream, charcoal brown, muted ochre, restrained desert blue accents, sparse dusty umber shadows
line_treatment: crisp engraved linework with fine historical map details and restrained hand-drawn marks
lighting: soft golden daylight with gentle archival warmth
frame_language: a recurring aged papyrus illustration window with softly worn deckled edges, engraved border marks, and a consistent parchment-like outer frame surrounding each scene
subtitle_reserve: a calm lower 8–10% papyrus field with minimal grain and no faces, hands, map labels, key objects, or important actions, reserved for two subtitle lines
subject_constraints: historical maps, garden discovery elements, books, manuscripts, maritime routes, ancient geographic illustrations, and archaeological-style artifacts are allowed; keep modern political imagery symbolic rather than documentary
historical_accuracy_note: Ancient Greek and Roman references, Persian Gulf mapping traditions, Strait of Hormuz geography, and historical cartographic elements should be depicted with period-appropriate materials and avoid implying that modern borders or labels existed unchanged in ancient eras
hero_rendering_in_world: the gardener keeps the same recognizable hair silhouette, beard, and overalls silhouette, translated into engraved brown ink lines with muted papyrus shading and simple historical illustration proportions
negative_constraints: no photorealism, no 3D CGI, no anime, no glossy digital painting, no modern infographic style, no futuristic elements
reason: This episode is driven by ancient maps, written records, and historical naming layers, making archaeological engraving the strongest fit. It reuses a suitable catalog style rather than creating a new one because the medium directly supports geography and history. Recent usage is lower priority here because the last two episodes used different visual families, avoiding immediate repetition.
